A tray of buns. Three rows of twelve. I split it in a tens part, and a ones part.
The tens part is three rows of ten. That is thirty.
The ones part is three rows of two. That is six.
I add the parts. Thirty and six is thirty-six.
Your turn. Four rows of thirteen. The parts are forty, and twelve. How many buns in all?
Fifty-two! A big tray is easy in parts.
Forty-eight buns, and four baskets. Every basket gets the same.
First I share the trays of ten. Each basket gets one tray. That is ten.
Then I share the eight loose buns. Each basket gets two more.
Ten and two is twelve. Forty-eight divided by four is twelve.
Your turn. Fourteen buns, four baskets. Each basket gets three. How many are left?
Two are left. Not enough to give every basket one more.
A loaf cut in four slices. One slice here, and two slices there.
The slices are the same size. So I just count them. One and two is three fourths.
Now one half, and one fourth. The slices are not the same size!
I cut the half again. One half is two fourths.
Your turn. Two fourths and one fourth. How many fourths is that?
Three fourths. Same size slices first. Then count.
This full tray is one. It has one hundred small squares.
A strip is ten squares. Ten strips fill the tray. One strip is one tenth.
Three strips is three tenths. We write zero point three.
One small square is one hundredth. Four strips and seven squares is zero point four seven.
Your turn. Which one is more?
Yes. Five strips is more than four strips and five squares.
